Pressing Rewind: The Universe Had a Beginning
In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. (Genesis 1:1)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you all! Let me start with a question: have you ever watched old videos of yourself as a little child? That chubby toddler wobbling across the screen is the very person sitting here today. Lots of families know that experience: everyone gathered around the old home movies, laughing until they cry.
Now imagine this. Suppose we filmed the entire history of the universe as a movie, and then pressed the “rewind” button. What would you see?

You would see every galaxy running backward, drawing closer and closer, packing tighter and tighter, until all of them were squeezed into one hot, dense starting point. And before that moment? Our telescopes can see nothing at all. That is where the film begins.

More than three thousand years ago, Moses wrote the first sentence of the Bible: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.” And twentieth-century astronomers spent decades, using the best instruments they had, to arrive at the same conclusion: the universe has not always been here. The universe had a beginning.

Today we are stepping together into the first gallery of the Cosmos Hall, to see how scientists discovered this step by step, and how this discovery helps us know better the God who was there “in the beginning.”
A red clue in the spectrum

The story begins with starlight. Astronomers found that the light from distant galaxies is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum. This is called “redshift.” Redshift means that a galaxy is moving away from us, and the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is receding.

How can we picture that? Imagine a loaf of raisin bread rising in your kitchen. As the dough slowly swells, if you were one of the raisins, you would see all the other raisins moving away from you, and the farther away they were, the faster they would recede.

The universe is like that dough. Here is the key point: the galaxies are not flying off in all directions through space; space itself is expanding. So next time you eat raisin bread, you can tell your family, “Did you know? This is a model of the universe.” I guarantee they will look at you with brand-new respect.

This discovery was not made by one person; it was more like a relay race. Beginning in 1912, American astronomer Vesto Slipher measured redshifts in the spectra of most spiral nebulae. In 1927, Belgian physicist Georges Lemaître derived from Einstein's equations that the universe is expanding. And here is something interesting: Lemaître was also a Catholic priest.

In 1929, Edwin Hubble confirmed with observational data that a galaxy's distance is proportional to its speed of recession. Later, in 2018, the International Astronomical Union recommended renaming this law the “Hubble–Lemaître law,” sharing the credit with that priest-scientist.

Think about it, friends: the universe is expanding; that is what we observe. So what happens if we play the film of that expansion backward? We come back to a starting point. An expanding universe is a universe with a “beginning.”
By Yahweh's word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth. … For he spoke, and it was done. He commanded, and it stood firm. (Psalm 33:6, 9)
Spiritual meaning: he spoke, and it was done

Brothers and sisters, everything we humans make is a rearrangement of materials that already exist. A chef needs ingredients to cook; a carpenter needs wood to build a table; even the most brilliant engineer can only rearrange things that are already there.

But the Bible says that God “spoke, and it was done.” Only God can bring “something” out of “nothing.” A universe that began to exist points to a cause outside the universe, one of immeasurable power. This is what Romans 1:20 means when it says that God's “everlasting power” is perceived through the things that are made.
Scientists then reasoned: if the universe began hot and dense, some “leftover warmth” should remain today.

In 1965, while Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson were calibrating an antenna at Bell Labs, they kept picking up a microwave hiss they simply could not get rid of, and it came evenly from every direction. At first they thought something was wrong with the antenna. But that hiss turned out to be the very afterglow left over from the beginning of the universe, now called the “cosmic microwave background radiation.” The two men received the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.
You see, sometimes the great discoveries God gives are hidden inside an annoying bit of noise. The “noise” in our lives that we find so irritating may also hide a voice God wants us to hear.

What is this afterglow like? It is like walking into a house after a great fire has gone out: you can no longer see the flames, but the walls are still faintly warm. Today this afterglow has cooled to about minus 270 degrees Celsius, yet it still fills the whole sky evenly.

In the 1990s, the COBE satellite measured the spectrum of this radiation and found that it matched the “blackbody” curve predicted by theory almost perfectly, at a temperature of about 2.725 K. There is another independent line of evidence too: the lightest elements in the universe. By mass, ordinary matter is about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium, exactly the ratio predicted by the “hot beginning” model.
Scientists did not welcome it at first

You might think that when scientists heard the universe had a beginning, they all applauded. Not at all. In 1917, Einstein deliberately added a “cosmological constant” to his equations to keep the universe static and unchanging.

British astronomer Fred Hoyle proposed the “steady-state theory,” which held that the universe had no beginning. On a 1949 BBC radio program he mockingly called his rivals' theory the “Big Bang.” Little did he know that this slightly teasing name would stick from then on. Only after the background radiation was discovered did the steady-state theory lose the support of most scholars.

Robert Jastrow, the founding director of NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies, called himself an agnostic. In his book God and the Astronomers he wrote that the scientist has scaled the mountains of ignorance and is about to conquer the highest peak, only to be greeted by a band of theologians who have been sitting there for centuries.
Before the mountains were born, before you had formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God. (Psalm 90:2)
Spiritual meaning: a garment wearing out

The second law of thermodynamics says that the usable energy in the universe keeps decreasing, like a garment slowly wearing out. Three thousand years ago the psalmist already painted this picture: “All of them will wear out like a garment… But you are the same. Your years will have no end.”

The universe grows old; it has a starting point and it is heading toward an end, but God does not. When our lives feel like a garment that gets more worn every day, as our work, our bodies and our relationships are all being used up, we can look up to the God who is “from everlasting to everlasting.” He does not wear out, and neither does his love.
At this point we need to do something very important: keep scientific fact and philosophical inference distinct. That is a way of honoring the truth.

The universe is expanding; the background radiation exists; the history of the observable universe can be traced back to an extremely hot, extremely dense early state. These are all very well-established observations. According to the standard cosmological model, the universe is about 13.787 billion years old, though different methods still give different values for the expansion rate. Scientists call this the “Hubble tension,” and it is still being studied.

In 2003, Borde, Guth and Vilenkin proved that a universe that has, on average, always been expanding cannot be extended infinitely into the past. But what happens at the scale of quantum gravity is still unsettled, and some scholars have proposed other models. We don't exaggerate, and we don't dodge.

In philosophy there is the “kalam cosmological argument.” It is very simple, just three sentences: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause.

The first sentence is everyday common sense. If a package suddenly appeared at your front door, you would not say, “It just popped up by itself.” The second sentence is supported by the scientific discoveries we just looked at. And the third lets us reasonably conclude that the cause of the universe cannot be part of the universe: this One must transcend time, space and matter, and must have chosen to create by his own will.
United on the core, gracious on the secondary

By the way, evangelical Christians hold different views on “how old the universe is.” Old-earth creationism accepts the age measured by astronomy and holds that the “days” of Genesis can be understood as long periods or as a literary framework; young-earth creationism, based on the genealogies and the literal meaning of “day,” holds that the universe is thousands of years old.

But on the fact that “the universe had a beginning and was created by God,” everyone is completely united. We are united on the core and gracious on the secondary matters. Brothers and sisters of different views can all stand together under the starry sky and marvel: the universe did not come from itself.

For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, … all things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things are held together. (Colossians 1:16–17)
Spiritual meaning: the cause has a name
Brothers and sisters, the Bible does not only tell us that the universe has a cause; it tells us the name of that cause. The Lord who existed before the universe began is Jesus Christ.

Even more wonderful, this Lord who is before time entered time for our sake, became a man, died on the cross and rose from the dead. The Creator is not only the cause of the universe; he is the Savior who longs to draw near to us. “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”
Change your perspective: from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one

We often say we need to change from a human perspective to God's perspective. Standing before the story of the universe's beginning, we can say: my troubles are big, but the God who created the universe is bigger. The problem hasn't disappeared, but it has been set inside a much bigger picture.
Return to our proper place: humility overcomes pride

What is pride? Pride is leaving our proper place and trying to take God's place. Without even noticing, we often want to be the “beginning” of our own lives, deciding everything for ourselves. Under the starry sky we learn humility: letting people be people, and letting God be God.

Since all things are held together in him, my family, my work and my tomorrow can all be handed over to his rule as well. Letting Jesus reign is not losing our freedom; it is coming back into the hands of the Lord who pressed the “start button.”

Here is a small action step for this week: pick one evening and look up at the sky for five minutes. Then find a friend and ask them one question: “Where do you think the universe came from?” You will find it is an easy conversation to start, and a deep one too.

Brothers and sisters, today we rewound the film of the universe all the way back to “the beginning.” Scientists took decades to get there, only to find that the Bible's first sentence had already said it.

The psalmist says, “When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him?” The Lord who created hundreds of billions of galaxies also knows your name.
Let's be still for a moment and think: before this Lord, who am I? Let us pray together.

When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him? (Psalm 8:3–4)

Lord, you are the beginning of all things. You spoke, and it was done; you commanded, and it stood firm. I confess that I often want to be my own lord, to control every part of my life. Today I return to my proper place as a creature: I let you be God, and I let you reign in my heart. Thank you, Lord who is before all things, for being willing to enter time and go to the cross for me. All glory belongs to you. In Jesus' name, Amen.

A Just-Right Universe: Who Set the Dials?
He has made the earth by his power. He has established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding has he stretched out the heavens. (Jeremiah 10:12)

Peace to you, friends! Has anyone ever been halfway through a shower when the hot water suddenly turned ice-cold, or the cold water suddenly turned scalding? I'm sure many of you have. In that moment you understand what a huge difference it makes when one little dial is turned a tiny bit too far one way or the other.

If the shower temperature is off, the worst that happens is a scream. But today I want to invite you to picture something much bigger: a control panel for the entire universe, with dozens of dials on it: the strength of gravity, the strength of electromagnetism, the mass ratio of the proton to the electron, and so on.

Physicists have found that if several of these dials were turned even a tiny bit, the universe would have no stable stars, no carbon, and no us. In other words, the fact that we can sit here today listening to a sermon, drinking coffee, or dozing off, is all because these dials “happen” to be set in exactly the right positions.
By wisdom Yahweh founded the earth. By understanding, he established the heavens. (Proverbs 3:19)
Today let's look together at a few of the dials on the universe's control panel, and then ask one question: who set these numbers?
1. The most astonishing dial: the cosmological constant

In the last unit we learned that the universe is expanding. Later, scientists discovered that the expansion is actually speeding up. What drives this accelerating expansion is called the “cosmological constant,” which some also call dark energy.

This number is extremely small, but it is not zero. Strangely, according to rough estimates from quantum physics, it ought to be about 10 to the 120th power times larger. How big is 10 to the 120th? It is a 1 followed by 120 zeros. Most of us start to get shaky hands after writing five or six zeros on a check; this number is so big you could never finish writing it.

Physicist Steven Weinberg pointed out that if the cosmological constant were a few hundred times larger than its actual value, the universe would expand too quickly for galaxies ever to form. No galaxies means no stars; no stars means no earth, and no you or me.
Hitting a bull's-eye on the far side of the universe

How precise is that? We can picture it like this: shoot an arrow from earth and try to hit a bull's-eye smaller than the eye of a needle on the far side of the universe. The value of the cosmological constant lands right in that bull's-eye.

Some of our brothers go to play darts, stand three meters from the board, can't hit it at all, and blame the darts for being too light. This arrow of the universe, though, crosses the entire cosmos and hits dead center.
Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you establish its dominion over the earth? (Job 38:33)
Spiritual meaning: from “heard of” to “now my eye sees”

In the book of Job, God speaks out of the whirlwind and asks Job a whole series of questions about heaven and earth. These questions are not meant to humiliate Job, but to open his eyes. When Job understood, he said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.”

Brothers and sisters, grasping the precision of the universe can move us from “knowing there is a God” to “meeting God.” When we see a precision that amazes even physicists, something inside us says: this is not random; behind this is a wise Lord.
Other numbers on the control panel
The cosmological constant is only one of them. There are several other just-right numbers; let me briefly introduce four.

First, the ratio of gravity to electromagnetism. It determines whether stars can burn steadily for a long time. If the sun burned itself out all at once, or kept flickering bright and dim, life on earth could not survive.

Second, the strong nuclear force. This is the force that binds atomic nuclei together, and its strength affects whether the chemical elements can form. Without elements there would be no water, no air, and no bodies for us.

Third, the density fluctuations in the early universe, about one part in 100,000. Too small, and matter could not clump into galaxies; too large, and most of it would collapse into black holes. It is like kneading dough for bread: if the flour is too dry it won't come together, and if it's too sticky it all turns into one gluey lump. It has to be just right.
Fourth, the dimensions of space. Three-dimensional space allows both planetary orbits and atoms to remain stable. We usually take it for granted, but even “three dimensions” is a gift.

Britain's Astronomer Royal, Martin Rees, wrote a book called Just Six Numbers, picking out six numbers that determine the shape of the universe. Astrophysicist Luke Barnes, in a 2012 review paper, surveyed many published studies on fine-tuning.

We also need to say honestly that scholars still debate the degree of “fine-tuning.” Some constants can change together and offset one another, and some estimates depend on particular models. But most physicists agree that, under the present laws of physics, the range that permits life is very narrow compared with the range of possible values.
He has made the earth by his power. He has established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding has he stretched out the heavens. (Jeremiah 10:12)
A precise clock makes us think of a clockmaker; a just-right universe leads us reasonably to a Creator of infinite wisdom.

And he did not merely make all things; he arranged the universe just right for life, and for us. It is like a mother who, before her child comes home, sets the room at the right temperature, warms up the food and makes the bed. The moment the child walks through the door, everything is ready. The universe is the home God prepared for us.

Sometimes children get so used to it that when they come home they just say, “I'm home,” disappear into their room and scroll on their phones, never wondering where that bowl of hot soup on the table came from. Aren't we often like that with the universe? Every day we enjoy steady sunlight, stable atoms and a stable earth, and we never once say thank you.
So today, let's pause right here and say to the God who set everything just right: “Lord, thank you. You thought of everything.”
With so many just-right numbers, how do scientists explain them? There are two main views.
The first is the design explanation: the values of the universe look carefully set, pointing to a wise and purposeful Designer. This is a philosophical inference drawn from observation.

The second is the multiverse explanation: perhaps there are countless universes, each with different values, and we just happen to live in one that fits. That sounds very imaginative, but for now it remains theoretical speculation with no direct observational evidence. And the mechanism that would produce a multiverse itself needs fine-tuning.

It is a bit like winning the lottery and having a friend say, “No big deal; there may be countless tickets in the world.” But then the question is: who designed and tuned the machine that prints all those countless tickets?

Interestingly, whichever explanation one takes, both admit that the universe's values “look as if they have been tuned.” The real question is: is this coincidence, one universe among countless others, or the intention of a Designer?

We don't say “science has proved God”; science doesn't work that way. But these discoveries really do point to a wise Creator. They give those who believe very good reasons, and they give those who are searching a very good place to start.
For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen. (Romans 11:36)
Spiritual meaning: your life is in his hands too
Brothers and sisters, the largest and the smallest numbers in the universe are all tuned just right in his hands. So what about your life?

The dials of your life, your family, your work, your health, the people you meet, are in his hands too. Some things you thought were chance turn out, when you look back, to have been God's arrangement. The God who tuned the universe will not fail to tune your life.

Maybe you feel that one of the dials in your life has been turned the wrong way: a lost job, a broken relationship, a prayer that still has no answer. When we can't understand, it is easy to think everything is out of control. But remember: our not being able to understand 10 to the 120th power doesn't mean the universe wasn't tuned; and our not understanding our present situation doesn't mean God is not in control.

Job couldn't understand either in the middle of his suffering. God did not give him a detailed explanation; instead he showed him the laws of heaven and earth. Job saw God, and his heart grew quiet. Sometimes what we need is not more answers, but to know better the God who holds the answers.

God set precise laws in the universe so the stars can burn steadily; he has also set the standard of truth for our lives in the Bible. The numbers of the universe can't be adjusted at random, and neither can the direction of our lives be adjusted by feelings. When the Bible is our standard, our lives will be “just right.”

We don't have to understand everything before we trust. Honestly, I can't work out 10 to the 120th power either. A wisdom that amazes even physicists is worthy of our confident surrender. Humility is not giving up on thinking; it is admitting that God's wisdom is greater than mine.
Let Jesus receive all the glory

When we see something exquisite, let's give the praise to the Designer, not to coincidence. It's the same in daily life: when things go well, don't just say “What luck!” Learn to say “Thank the Lord.” Let Jesus receive all the glory.

This week's action: write down three things you once thought were coincidences but now see as God's arrangement, and share one of them with a friend. You'll find that once you start counting, there is more grace than you imagined.

Friends, next time you adjust the water temperature in the shower, I hope you'll remember today's message: one small dial can decide between comfort and a scream, and the dials of the universe decide whether there are stars and whether there is life.

The God who established the world by his wisdom and stretched out the heavens by his understanding is watching over you with that same wisdom. Let's be still for a moment and think: what is one thing in my life that I thought was chance, but was really God's arrangement?

Lord, in your wisdom you tuned the whole universe; from the largest galaxy to the smallest atom, everything is just right in your hands. You also watch over every detail of my life. I confess that I often rely on my own cleverness and try to adjust everything myself. Today I lay down my own cleverness and trust in your wisdom. To you be the glory forever. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Three Thousand Galaxies in a Grain of Sand: The Vast Starry Sky

Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these, who brings out their army by number. He calls them all by name. By the greatness of his might, and because he is strong in power, not one is lacking. (Isaiah 40:26)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! When you were a child, did you ever lie on the grass or on a rooftop and try to count the stars? You'd get to twenty-something and start losing track: “Did I already count that one?” In the end you'd give up and fall asleep.
Today we are going to do something bolder: not just count stars, but measure, step by step, from the earth to the edge of the observable universe, measuring the heavens made by God's hand.

Let me give you a feel for it first. How fast is light? Light can circle the earth seven and a half times in one second. In the blink of an eye, light has already gone around the earth several times. Yet light from the farthest reaches of the universe has traveled for more than ten billion years to reach our eyes.
Friends, this is the world we are entering today. Please fasten your seatbelts; we're about to take off.

Let's start close to home. The sunlight that falls on your face every morning takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to travel from the sun to the earth. In other words, the sun you see is always the sun of eight-some minutes ago.

Leaving the solar system, the nearest star is called Proxima Centauri, about 4.24 light-years away. Light takes more than four years to get there. If you mailed your family a “postcard of light” from Proxima Centauri today, they wouldn't get it for more than four years; by then your kids might have graduated from elementary school.
Third stop: the Milky Way and Andromeda

Our own Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across and holds 100 to 400 billion stars. What does a hundred billion mean? Even if you counted one star per second, without eating or sleeping, your hair would turn gray before you finished.
Farther out, our neighbor the Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away. If you see it tonight from somewhere very dark, the light you see set out a very, very long time ago.

The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across. Someone might ask: isn't the universe only a little over ten billion years old? How can it be larger than “the age of the universe times the speed of light”? Because while the light was on its way, space itself was expanding. It's like running on a track that keeps stretching longer: by the time you reach the finish line, the starting line is far behind you.

Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and marked off the sky with his span, and calculated the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance? (Isaiah 40:12)
Spiritual meaning: marking off the sky with his span

Friends, open your hand and look at the distance from your thumb to your little finger. That is your “span.” We use our span to measure a book or a table. Isaiah says God marked off the entire sky with the span of his hand.

We have gone to such lengths, measuring the universe in light-years, and after 93 billion light-years we still haven't finished. But in God's eyes, all of the heavens are just the width of his hand. However big the universe is, his power is bigger still.
2. A patch of sky the size of a grain of sand
Ten days with the Hubble telescope
In 1995, the Hubble Space Telescope did something that seemed very strange. It pointed at a tiny, seemingly empty patch of sky near the Big Dipper and photographed it continuously for ten days.

How tiny was that patch? About one 24-millionth of the whole sky, like looking at a grain of sand on your fingertip with your arm stretched out. Many people thought: what's the point of photographing an empty piece of sky?
When the images came back, everyone was stunned. In that sand-grain-sized patch of sky, about three thousand galaxies appeared.
If each galaxy were a city, that sand-grain-sized patch of sky would be packed with three thousand cities, and each city would be home to a hundred billion stars or more.

The place we thought was empty was actually full of God's works. Brothers and sisters, our lives also have places that look “empty,” as if there is nothing there, as if God is absent. But if we are willing to be still and keep gazing, we often discover that those places are actually full of God's grace.
So how many galaxies are there?

So how many galaxies are there in the whole observable universe? Estimates range from several hundred billion to more than a trillion. A 2016 study estimated that there may be as many as two trillion; in 2021, New Horizons measured the cosmic background light from beyond Pluto and came up with a much lower estimate, about several hundred billion.

Estimates from different methods still differ widely. That is not a failure of science; it is science's ongoing process of correction at work. Let's be honest: humanity, with its best telescopes, still cannot count how many galaxies there really are.
He counts the number of the stars. He calls them all by their names. (Psalm 147:4)
Spiritual meaning: the God who knows every name

We can't count the galaxies, yet God can call every star by name. Think about it: some of us can't even remember our coworkers' names, and in the elevator all we can manage is an awkward “Oh, hey, hi!” But God calls by name every single star in hundreds of billions, even trillions, of galaxies, and not one is missing.

In the Bible, “calling by name” means more than remembering a name; it carries the sense of knowing, caring for and leading. Isaiah says God “brings out their army by number,” like a shepherd leading out his flock each morning, calling the roll one by one, never missing a single sheep.

If God pays such attention to the stars, how could he not pay attention to a person made in his image, a person for whom he sent his only Son to lay down his life? You are not a nameless number in the universe; you are a child whom God calls by name.
3. After the stars, a word for the weary
The vastness of the universe does not mean people don't matter
At this point some of you may feel a kind of sinking feeling: the universe is so big and I am so small; what am I? God is so busy, running all those galaxies; how would he have time for me?

That is a very real feeling. But we need to be clear about one thing: the vastness of the universe does not mean human beings are unimportant. On the contrary, the Bible says the God who made all the host of heaven cares especially for people. This is a declaration of faith, and it is the heart of today's message.
What comes next in the same passage

The most beautiful thing is the context of Isaiah 40. Right after Isaiah says, “Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these,” whom does he turn to next? Not to astronomers, not to kings, but to people who are weary.

Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel, “My way is hidden from Yahweh, and the justice due me is disregarded by my God”? … He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might. (Isaiah 40:27, 29)

The Israelites back then felt that God couldn't see their way, that God didn't care about the injustice they suffered. So Isaiah had them look up at the stars: how could the God who calls every star by name ever forget you?
Spiritual meaning: the God who counts the stars also counts your tears
The God who counts the stars also counts your tears. He can measure the heavens, and he can measure the burden in your heart. In his hands, your burden is not heavy.
But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint. (Isaiah 40:31)

We often say our focus should not be on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances, but on Jesus. When we keep staring at our troubles, they look bigger and bigger; when we lift our eyes to the Lord who is greater than the universe, our hearts find rest.
From an earthly perspective to a heavenly one

Notice that the problem may not get smaller, but we see that God is bigger. That is a change of perspective. The same trouble that looks like a mountain in my eyes is only a speck of dust in the hands of the God who marks off the heavens with his span.

Under the vast starry sky, no one can go on thinking they are great. The face we fight to save, the achievements we compare, the arguments we have to win, all look tiny in a universe 93 billion light-years across. Humility is not low self-esteem; it is seeing our true size, and seeing God's true greatness.

Picture a brother who is arguing with his wife and about to explode. He steps out onto the balcony, looks up at the sky, and when he comes back in, half his anger is gone. Why? Because he suddenly realizes that getting red in the face over who forgot to take out the trash is a little funny under a sky full of stars. Of course, the trash still needs to go out.
What humility brings is often not loss but freedom. When I no longer need to be the center of the universe, I can relax a little, love people well, and let myself be loved well by God.

This week's action: think of a friend who is going through a weary season, send them Isaiah 40:26–31, and pray for them. You may never know it, but your one message could be their strength for the week.

Brothers and sisters, if the weather is clear tonight, please look up at the sky and try counting how many stars you can see. It's fine if you can't count them all, because there is One who remembers every one of their names.
And please remember: he can call every star by name, and he can call you by name too. Let's quietly reflect: how big are my troubles when set within the universe? And how big are they before God?

Lord, you mark off the heavens with your span; you count the number of the stars and call them all by their names. I am so small before you, and yet you remember my name and you count my tears. Let There Be Light: A Just-Right Window
God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. (Genesis 1:3)

Peace to you, friends! Have you ever been through a power outage? Especially when the power suddenly goes out at night, and the whole family is groping around in the dark: someone bumps into the corner of the table, someone steps on the cat, and then someone shouts, “Where's the flashlight?” Only when the lights come back on does everyone breathe a sigh of relief.
That's the moment we realize how important light is. We live in light every day, yet we hardly ever think about it.

Take a look around you. Every color you see right now, the colors of clothes, the color of the walls, the smiles on the faces of the brothers and sisters beside you, all of it is light. The first words God spoke in creation, in the Bible, were: “Let there be light.”
Today let's look at what mysteries are hidden in this light we use every day but rarely think about, and how it speaks of God's goodness and wisdom.
The speed of light in a vacuum is 299,792,458 meters per second. This number never changes; it is so stable that since 1983 people have simply used it to define how long “one meter” is.

Think about it: the most basic ruler we use to measure length is actually defined by light. The speed limit of the whole universe is light. Highways have speed cameras, and the universe also has a top speed limit, one that nobody can break.
Everything we see is the past

Light is fast, but its journey still takes time. So light is like the universe's messenger, delivering letters for faraway stars. Because the messenger has to travel a distance, every star we see is showing us “how it used to look.”

For example, light from the Andromeda Galaxy has been traveling for about 2.5 million years. The Andromeda you see tonight is a letter it mailed 2.5 million years ago. The farther we look, the older the universe we see. Astronomers holding their telescopes are really reading letter after letter sent from the past.

This reminds me that when we look at people, we often see them “as they used to be,” too. We remember the wrong someone did in the past and keep seeing them through that impression. But God's grace may have been at work in them for a long time, and they are no longer the same. May we be willing, when we look at others, to give them a chance to be made new.
God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. (1 John 1:5)
Spiritual meaning: the God with no darkness at all
Brothers and sisters, light is one of the most stable and dependable things in the universe, so stable it can serve as a standard. The Bible says that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
Our human hearts change: passionate today, cold tomorrow. But God's holiness and goodness have no shadow and no variation. He is the most dependable “ruler” in our lives.
The rainbow is only a small slice

The light the human eye can see is only a very narrow slice of the whole electromagnetic spectrum. Visible light has wavelengths of roughly 380 to 750 nanometers. The electromagnetic spectrum is very, very wide, and what we can see is just one thin slit within it.

Let's do a little exercise together: close your eyes, count silently to five, then slowly open them. Everything you just saw again is all squeezed into that thin slit. Such a narrow slit, and yet it holds all the beauty we will ever see in our lives.
You might think: what a pity; why didn't God let us see more? But the next discovery will make you think this slit was opened in exactly the right place.
Four things through the same window

Notice these four things. First, the band where the sun gives off the most energy falls right here. Second, earth's atmosphere is almost transparent in this band, while absorbing much of the harmful ultraviolet and some of the infrared. Third, water is transparent only in this band, which lets life in the oceans carry out photosynthesis. Fourth, what our eyes can see is exactly this band.
The peak of the sun's light, the atmosphere's window, water's window, and the eye's window: four windows that almost overlap in the same narrow opening.

It's as if you were mailing a package from Taipei to Kaohsiung, and the post office's opening hours, the truck's departure time, the time the recipient is home, and the moment you finished wrapping the package all lined up in the same minute. One thing lining up is luck; when four things line up at once, you start to wonder whether someone arranged it in advance.

Even more interesting, the energy range photosynthesis needs and the energy range needed by the light-sensitive molecules in our eyes also fall within the same window. Biochemist Michael Denton calls this a chain of astonishing “coincidences.”

We should also say honestly that each of these phenomena has a physical explanation; for example, the energies at which molecules absorb light naturally fall in this range. But the real question is: why do the laws of nature happen to make so many conditions favorable to life at the same time? That leads us reasonably to conclude that there is purpose and design behind it. This is a philosophical inference, and scholars differ on what it means.
In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it. (John 1:4–5)
Light makes all things visible, and it lets life grow. God placed light on the first day of creation, as if to say, “I am giving you a world you can see and live in.”

This is God's goodness. He did not just give light; he gave just the right light. He did not just give us eyes; he made the eyes, the air, the seawater and the sunlight all work together. He is like a thoughtful father who has prepared everything just right.

Think about it: if water only let other bands of light through, the oceans would be pitch black; if the atmosphere blocked visible light, the ground would be forever overcast; if our eyes could only see light the sun rarely gives off, the world would look dim to us. But God made all of this line up.
Every day we open our eyes and see colors, see our family's faces, see green leaves outside the window. None of this is to be taken for granted. Every time we see, it is a gift.
3. In the beginning he lit the universe; today he lights the heart
The Gospel of John opens by taking us straight back to Genesis: “In him was life, and the life was the light of men.” This “him” is Jesus Christ.
Later Jesus said with his own lips:
I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life. (John 8:12)
The apostle Paul goes a step further and connects the first light of Genesis with the moment a person comes to faith.
seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. (2 Corinthians 4:6)

Friends, in the beginning God said in the darkness, “Let there be light,” and the universe lit up. Today, when a person's heart is in darkness, God can say the same, “Let there be light,” and that heart lights up. In the beginning God lit up the universe; today he lights up the human heart.
Spiritual meaning: let the light into every corner

But when light comes in, it can sometimes make us uncomfortable. It's like when you still want to sleep in and someone in your family throws open the curtains, and you pull the blanket over your head. John says, “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it.”

There may be a corner of our hearts where we don't want to let the light in: someone we haven't forgiven, a hidden habit, a wound we don't want to face. Today God gently invites us to draw back the curtains.

Please don't be afraid. God's light is not the glaring lamp in an interrogation room, meant to expose you until you have nowhere to hide; his light is more like the morning sun, which shines in to heal and to make things grow. Plants need light to carry out photosynthesis, and our hearts need God's light to grow.

Picture a room whose windows have been shut for years. The dust on the table is thick, and there's a musty smell in the corner, and the owner has never dared to open the windows for fear that people will see what a mess it is. But what actually makes the room clean is not keeping the windows shut; it's opening them, letting the sunlight and fresh air in, and cleaning bit by bit. Our hearts are the same.

That corner you've always kept hidden may be exactly the place God most wants to heal. When we are willing to confess in the light and entrust things to him in the light, darkness no longer has power to control us.
The Holy Spirit is my guide

Light shines on everything not to show off, but so people can see the path clearly. We often don't know what our next step should be. At times like that, don't just grope forward in the dark by your own feelings; ask the Holy Spirit to light up your next step. The Holy Spirit is our guide, and he will give us just the right amount of light, enough for the next step.

It's like driving a mountain road at night. The headlights can't reach the top of the mountain; they only light a short stretch ahead of you. But as long as you keep driving, the light keeps shining ahead of you, one stretch after another, and you'll get home safely. God rarely lights up the whole road at once, but he never leaves those who follow him without light.
Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path. (Psalm 119:105)
Live out the life of Christ
Jesus not only said that he is the light of the world; he also said to us:

You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can't be hidden. Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven. (Matthew 5:14–16)

Notice the last sentence: the purpose of the light is for people to give glory to the Father in heaven. Letting Jesus receive all the glory is not about us shining and becoming famous, but about people seeing God because of us.

Light does not shine for itself; it lights up others. You've never seen a lamp shining at itself, have you? The self-emptied life is like that: not centered on ourselves, but living so that because we are there, other people's lives are a little brighter and a little warmer.

A mirror gives off no light of its own, but when it faces the sun, it can reflect light into dark corners. We are the same: our light is not our own; it comes from the Lord. The more we face him, the more we can carry his light to the people around us who need it.

Thank you for giving us light on the very first day of creation, and thank you for shining in my heart so that I may know your glory. Please shine into the corners of my heart I'm still unwilling to open, and make me a light for others, so that people may see my good works and glorify our Father in heaven. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Dust Fired in the Stars: The Furnace of the Stars
when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy? (Job 38:7)
Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Let's begin with a small gesture: put your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat. Thump, thump, thump. Now, I have some astonishing news for you.

The iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones, the carbon in every one of your cells: none of it was made on earth. It was forged in the cores of ancient stars, at temperatures of many millions of degrees.

So next time someone asks you, “Where do you come from?” you can answer very poetically, “The stuff I'm made of came from the stars.” Of course, after you say that, don't forget to add who it was that had the stars forge those materials.
Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul. (Genesis 2:7)
God formed man from “the dust of the ground,” and that dust, it turns out, was fired in the furnaces of the stars. Today, let's step together into this great furnace of the universe.
1. Where do the elements come from?
Everything around us is made of elements. So where did these elements come from? Scientists have found that the universe seems to have three different factories.
The first factory operated in the first few minutes after the universe began. That's when the lightest elements formed: hydrogen, helium, and a little lithium.

The second factory is in the cores of stars. There, lighter nuclei fuse into heavier ones: carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, all the way up to iron, are forged here. A star is like a gigantic steel mill, burning day and night without stopping.

The third factory is the most spectacular. Elements heavier than iron, such as gold and iodine, are produced in supernova explosions and neutron star collisions. So, sisters, the gold ring on your finger came to you through the most earth-shattering collisions in the universe. Next time your husband gives you gold jewelry, what he's really giving you is a small souvenir of an exploding star.
In 1957, Margaret and Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle published a classic paper that fully explained how stars make the elements.

Then in 2017, astronomers for the first time observed a collision of two neutron stars with both gravitational waves and light, and saw with their own eyes heavy elements being formed. A theory written on paper decades earlier was seen in the sky.
when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy? (Job 38:7)
Spiritual meaning: a gift long in the making

Before human beings appeared, stars had burned and exploded generation after generation, preparing the materials for life. This shows us how God works: he is never in a hurry, and he thinks of everything.

It's like a mother preparing a Lunar New Year feast for her children: she doesn't start on New Year's Eve; she starts days before, shopping, marinating the meat, simmering the soup. What God prepares for us is earlier and more thorough than we can imagine. Long, long before you were born, he was already preparing for you.

Of all the elements, carbon is especially important. Every cell in our bodies depends on carbon. But to form carbon, three helium nuclei have to collide almost at the same moment, which should be extremely difficult.

How difficult? Imagine a huge public square, and you need three strangers, each walking their own way, to bump into one another at the same spot at the same instant. Getting two people to bump into each other is hard enough; getting three to collide at once is so unlikely you'd want to give up.

In 1953, British astronomer Fred Hoyle made a bold inference. He said that since there is so much carbon in the universe, and since we are alive, the carbon nucleus must have a state at a specific energy, about 7.65 million electron volts, for carbon to be produced in large amounts.

It's a bit like him saying, “There must be a special meeting point in that square where the three people happen to meet.” Laboratory experiments soon found exactly that state, and today it is called the “Hoyle state.”

Most interesting of all, Hoyle himself did not believe in God. He's the same scientist who jokingly called his rivals' theory the “Big Bang.” Yet in 1981 he wrote that a common-sense interpretation of the facts suggests that a superintellect has “monkeyed” with physics, as well as with chemistry and biology.

We also need to say honestly that later studies have shown the yields of carbon and oxygen are quite sensitive to the energy of the Hoyle state and the strength of the nuclear force, though precise estimates of that sensitivity are still debated. We don't overstate the case, but these discoveries really do point to a wise Designer.
For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust. (Psalm 103:14)
Spiritual meaning: God knows we are dust
Brothers and sisters, this verse is so tender. God knows how we are made; he remembers that we are dust.

So when we are weak, when we fall, when we can't do it, God doesn't stand to the side shaking his head and saying, “How can you be so hopeless?” Instead he says, “I know. You're made of dust.” The God who prepared that dust grain by grain with his own hands understands our limits best and is the most patient with us.

It's like a potter who knows full well that the clay in his hands can crack or collapse, so he doesn't lose his temper with the clay; he kneads it again and shapes it again, time after time. God is like that with us. If you feel today that you've failed yet again, God has not given up on this lump of clay. He is still shaping you.

And a God who was willing to prepare such intricate conditions in the universe just so carbon could form, how could he be careless with your life? He is this careful at the level of the atom, so he will surely be just as careful in your life.
We are dust, and that keeps us humble. But the story doesn't stop there. Genesis says God “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.”

Dust plus God's breath makes a human being. We are small, yet treasured by God; we are dust, yet we carry God's breath. We need to remember both together: remember only the dust, and we sink into low self-worth; remember only the breath, and we become proud. Remember both, and we stand in the right place.
The differing glory of the stars
When Paul spoke about the resurrection, he also used the stars as an illustration.
There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for one star differs from another star in glory. (1 Corinthians 15:41)
Paul uses the differing glory of the stars to explain the glory of the resurrection body. We who came from dust will, through Christ, one day receive glorious, imperishable bodies.

Think about it: dust forged in the furnace of the stars, a human being formed from the dust, and then the glory of the resurrection revealed in that human being. God's story is a story from stars to dust, and from dust to glory.
Spiritual meaning: you are a work God carefully prepared

So however ordinary or unremarkable you may feel today, please remember: every atom in your body has gone through God's long and careful preparation. You were not thrown together at random; you are a work God carefully prepared.

Humility overcomes pride. Our bodies, the very stuff we are made of, were all received; not one bit of it did we make ourselves. That being so, what do we have to boast about? When we feel like boasting, let's think of the furnace of the stars, and we'll grow quiet.

At the same time, we don't need to feel worthless. We are made in God's image, with God's breath within us. When the world measures you by your grades, your salary or your looks, remember God's verdict on you: you are someone he breathed life into.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry

God spent ages preparing the materials of life; he is never in a hurry. We often want to see results fast and rush into lots of ministry. But the 321 order is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Let's be patient too, and let God shape our lives slowly, just as the stars slowly forged carbon. Good things are worth waiting for.

We often want things “instant”: instant character, instant spiritual maturity, instant revival. But the furnace of the stars tells us that God likes to work through time. For a person's life to be refined by God often takes high heat, and a long wait as well.
So if you feel you're in the furnace right now, if the pressure is great and the fire is hot, please don't lose heart. It may be that God is forging something very precious in you.

When the universe began, the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy. Today, let us who came from dust yet carry God's breath sing to him together as well.

You know how I am made and remember that I am dust, yet you still breathed your breath into me. My life is your gift, and I want to offer it back to you for your use. In Jesus' name, Amen.

A Window God Opened: A Place to See the Universe
that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. (Acts 17:27)

Peace to you, friends! When you go to a concert or a ball game, what do you care about most? Your seat, of course. Get a good seat, and you see everything clearly; get a seat behind a pillar, and you spend the whole event looking at the pillar while the person next to you says, “Wow, did you see that play?”

Today I want to tell you that we humans seem to have been given an excellent ticket in the universe. Earth is not only fit to live on; it also happens to be an excellent place to observe the universe.

Let's start with something truly amazing. The sun's diameter is about 400 times the moon's, and the sun is also about 400 times farther from the earth than the moon is. The two factors of 400 cancel out, so from earth the moon can cover the sun exactly, without covering too much.

It's like holding up a small coin at arm's length and finding it exactly blocks a streetlight in the distance: not too big, not too small, just right. This means that during a total solar eclipse, scientists can see the corona around the sun, and can even see stars next to the sun in the daytime.
God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years; (Genesis 1:14)
1. The door to science that an eclipse opened
This “just right” is not only beautiful; it also did science a big favor.

In 1919, British astronomer Arthur Eddington and his colleagues used a total solar eclipse to photograph stars near the sun. They found that starlight passing the sun was bent, and that the amount of bending matched exactly the prediction of Einstein's general relativity.

This observation made relativity world-famous. Think about it: if the moon were a bit bigger, it would have blocked the starlight near the sun as well; if it were a bit smaller, the sun's light would have been too bright to see the nearby stars at all. Either way, this observation would have been very hard to carry out.

Imagine how those astronomers felt. They had their instruments ready and their eyes fixed on the sky, waiting for those few brief moments when the moon would cover the sun. Miss it, and they'd have to wait for the next chance. And the universe had long since opened that door for them, just waiting for someone to push it.
Living in just the right era

There's something even more amazing. The moon moves about 3.8 centimeters farther from the earth each year; this has been measured by laser ranging. In the distant past, the moon was closer; in the far future it will be farther away, and then there will be no more perfect total eclipses.
In other words, human beings happen to live in the era when perfect total eclipses can be seen. It's like arriving at a concert just as the best song of the night begins.

Have you ever wondered: why us? Why is it the people of this era who get to see the moon exactly cover the sun? We don't need to overstate the answer, but at the very least we can stop and say, “Lord, thank you for letting me live at a time when I can see all this.”
Spiritual meaning: lights in the sky as signs

Genesis says the lights in the sky are to be “for signs.” God made the sun, moon and stars not only to give light and divide day from night, but also for people to observe and understand. A total eclipse is like a sign God has written in the sky, letting humanity read more of the mysteries of the universe.
2. A good seat in the Milky Way
Not downtown, not in the wilderness
It isn't only the positions of the earth and moon that are just right; our solar system's location in the Milky Way is special too.

The solar system lies between the Milky Way's spiral arms. It's not in a crowded, dangerous place like the galactic core, nor at the edge where heavy elements are scarce. Astronomers call such a region the “galactic habitable zone.”

It's like house hunting. Live right in the busiest downtown, and you get chaotic traffic, lots of noise and plenty of danger; move too far out into the wilderness, and it's an hour's drive just to buy groceries, and supplies are scarce. The best place is a neighborhood that's quiet yet close to everything you need. Our solar system lives in just that kind of good neighborhood in the Milky Way.
We should also say honestly that scholars are still debating how large the galactic habitable zone really is.
Even more interesting, this location also gives us a clear view, less obscured by dust, of distant galaxies and the cosmic background radiation.

Astronomer Guillermo Gonzalez and philosopher Jay Richards have proposed that the places best suited for life also happen to be best suited for observation, and that this does not look like coincidence.

Of course, some have offered criticisms. Critics see this as a “selection effect”: observers able to think about these questions could only ever appear in suitable places, so there's no need to be surprised.

To put that criticism in an everyday example: you only say “Hello?” on phone calls that actually connect. So every time you say “Hello?” the call has gone through, and there's nothing strange about that. It's a very clever point, and we should take it seriously.

Supporters reply that a selection effect can explain why we live in a habitable place, but it doesn't necessarily explain why the same place is also suited for observation. This is a disputed philosophical argument, and we lay it honestly before you. But it does lead us reasonably to think that God not only gave us a home, but also gave us a place from which we can see his works.
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge. (Psalm 19:1–2)
Brothers and sisters, God did not only give people a home; he also gave them a window, so they could look out on the universe and understand his works.
The heavens speak every day, and every night they display knowledge. God is not a God who hides; he is a God who wants to be found. He has put us in a seat where we can hear the heavens speaking.

Think about it: if God had only wanted to give us somewhere to survive, he could easily have put us in some corner surrounded by dust where we could see nothing at all. We could still eat, sleep and work, but we would never know that there are hundreds of billions of galaxies out there. But God did not do that.

He is like a host who invites friends to his home, and not only prepares the meal but deliberately saves the best window seat for his guests, draws back the curtains and says, “Look how beautiful the view is.” He wants us not only to live, but to see, to marvel, and then to know him.
3. He is not far from each one of us
In Acts 17, Paul arrives in Athens. There were many philosophers there who didn't know the Bible or the God of Israel. How did Paul speak to them?

He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. (Acts 17:26–27)

Paul began with the created world they were familiar with and ended with Jesus rising from the dead. From the things that are made all the way to the Savior: that is exactly the path this app, Creation Speaks, follows. Every step we have taken today in the Cosmos Hall follows Paul's path too.

Notice what Paul says: God “determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings.” The era you were born into, the city you live in, the family you belong to: none of these are accidents.

Some people say, “How did I end up born into this family?” Others say, “How did I end up assigned to this department?” But the Bible tells us God determined all of this with a purpose: “that they should seek the Lord.”
Spiritual meaning: reaching out and finding him

“Reach out for him” paints a vivid picture, like someone groping with their hand in the dark. God says that if you only reach out, you will find he is not far from you at all. He is not a God who lives on the far side of some distant galaxy; he is right beside you.

When you were little and woke up in the middle of the night to a pitch-black room, did you ever reach out beside the bed, feeling around for your mom's hand? When you finally found that warm hand, you felt completely safe. Mom had been right there all along; you just couldn't see her. God is like that. He has always been there, just waiting for you to reach out.
As Jesus said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” This God has been waiting all along for you to reach out.

God has placed me in my family, my workplace and my city, and those places are territory of his kingdom. You were not “dumped” there; you were “sent” there. With one purpose: to build God's kingdom system, starting within your own boundaries.

My boundaries are not an accident but his arrangement. Rather than constantly complaining about my seat, I would do better to obey him in this seat. Letting Jesus reign means admitting: Lord, you put me here, so here I will be faithful.

We often think we need to change positions before God can use us: find a better job, move to a better city, wait until the kids are grown. But God placed the earth in a good spot in the Milky Way, and he has also placed you in a good spot in your life. The seat you're in right now is the place best suited for you to see him, and best suited for you to serve him.

God lets people “reach out for him and find him”; he opened a window. We can also become a window through which others come to know God. Your coworkers, neighbors and family may never read the Bible, but they are reading you every day. Let them see God's goodness through your life.

A window is not itself the view; its value lies in letting people see the view outside. When people look through us and see God rather than ourselves, we have become a good window. So let's keep that window polished: a little less complaining, a little more patience; a little less of self, a little more of Christ.

A Universe That Keeps the Rules: The Ordinances of Heaven and Earth
It is because of Yahweh's loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn't fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness. (Lamentations 3:22–23)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Let me ask you: are the buses near your home on time? If the buses where you live are punctual, if they say 3:05 and show up at 3:05, your life feels a lot more secure. But if the bus schedule depends entirely on the driver's mood, sometimes early, sometimes late, sometimes not at all, you'd be anxious every time you left the house.
So what kind of bus is our universe? The answer: astonishingly punctual.
In 1846, before any astronomer had seen Neptune, they worked out with pen and paper where it should be. Then they pointed the telescope in that direction, and there Neptune was, not a moment late.

If you were that astronomer, pointing your telescope at the spot you had calculated on paper and seeing that planet really there, how would you feel? I think you'd probably shout, “It's really there!” It's the joy of discovering that the universe truly keeps its word.

In 2015, scientists detected gravitational waves given off by the merger of two black holes more than a billion years ago. And these waves had been predicted by Einstein's equations back in 1916. A prediction written on paper rang out on the instruments nearly a century later. The universe keeps its rules, and keeps them astonishingly well.
While the earth remains, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease. (Genesis 8:22)
Today let's look at this rule-keeping universe, and at the faithful God behind it.

When astronomers analyze the spectra of distant galaxies, they find something very important: atoms there absorb and emit light exactly as they do in laboratories on earth. The laws of physics billions of light-years away are the same as the laws here.

Why is that such a big deal? Imagine if every part of the universe had different rules: gravity pulls down here, but pushes sideways over there. Scientists couldn't study anything, because what they learned here wouldn't count anywhere else.
It's like a dictionary. Whether you open the same dictionary in Taipei or in London, every word means the same thing. Every corner of the universe uses the same “dictionary of laws.”

We should also say honestly that whether the physical constants have changed very slightly over the history of the universe is still a research question. Current observations restrict any possible change in the fine-structure constant to a very small range, and there is as yet no accepted evidence of change. In other words, so far not a single word in the universe's dictionary has been found to have changed.

Picture a chef. If, in his kitchen, salt were salty today and sweet tomorrow, and the fire were hot today and not tomorrow, he could never cook a single dish. It's precisely because the rules are stable that a chef can develop his craft, scientists can do research, and we can go through each day with peace of mind.

Yahweh, who gives the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, who stirs up the sea, so that its waves roar; Yahweh of Armies is his name, says: “If these ordinances depart from before me,” says Yahweh, “then the offspring of Israel also will cease from being a nation before me forever.” (Jeremiah 31:35–36)
Spiritual meaning: the universe as collateral

Friends, this passage is so beautiful. God uses the laws of the universe as a guarantee of his promises. It's as if he were saying, “Look at the sun and moon in the sky. As long as they keep to their ordinances, my covenant with you will not fail.”

When we humans guarantee something, we find a person with good credit to co-sign. When God guarantees something, he signs with the whole universe. So every sunrise speaks of God's faithfulness. Tomorrow morning when the sun comes up, it will be telling you too: God's promises still stand.
Next I want to ask a question that may sound a bit strange: why does mathematics work?

Many of us suffered through math at school, often thinking, “What will I ever use this for?” But physicists have found that mathematics worked out by people on paper somehow describes the motions of distant heavenly bodies with precision. That is exactly how Neptune was calculated.

In 1960, Nobel laureate in physics Eugene Wigner wrote a famous essay describing the effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences as “unreasonable.” What he meant was: it works so well it hardly makes sense. Why should something thought up in the human brain match the universe?

Next time your child is doing math homework and complains, “What's the point of learning this?” you can tell them: these symbols once helped people find a planet no one had ever seen. Maybe they'll do two more problems. Then again, maybe not.
The conviction of the pioneers of modern science

For the pioneers of modern science, the answer was actually quite clear. People like Kepler and Newton believed the universe was made by a rational God, and was therefore worth studying and able to be understood.

To them, studying nature meant thinking the Creator's thoughts after him. It's like reading a good book: you want to get to know the author. The more you understand the universe, the more you want to know the God who wrote its laws.

So faith and science are not enemies. For these pioneers, it was precisely because they believed in a rational God that they had the confidence to study the universe, believing it was worth spending a lifetime calculating, measuring and observing. If the universe were random, studying it would be like trying to read a poem in a pile of gibberish; it's precisely because the universe has an Author that it can be read.
Spiritual meaning: a rational and faithful Creator

Why does the universe have order? Why can the universe be understood? This leads us reasonably to conclude that the best explanation is a rational and faithful Creator. This is a philosophical inference, not a laboratory measurement, but it is a very powerful inference.
Science is possible because the universe is orderly; the universe is orderly because the God who made it is faithful.
Not a machine that runs by itself
Some people think that after God made the universe, he left it running on its own like a wound-up clock and went off to rest. But what the Bible tells us is far more intimate than that.
His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power. (Hebrews 1:3)
What scientists call the “laws of nature,” the Bible calls Jesus' “word of his power.” The universe is not a machine that runs by itself; it is upheld by Christ at every moment.
It's like a father holding his child. The child sleeps soundly in his father's arms, not because the child is floating in midair on his own, but because the father's arms have never let go.
Every day we see the sun rise, the seasons turn, and gravity keep us firmly on the ground. None of this is to be taken for granted; it is because Christ's hands have never let go.

Do you remember learning to ride a bike as a child? Your dad held the back of the seat and said, “Go ahead, I've got you.” You wobbled all over the place, but you never fell. Only years later did you realize that the reason you didn't fall back then was that those hands were always there.
Spiritual meaning: he upholds you too
Brothers and sisters, God never breaks faith in the universe, so how could his promises to you fail?

You may be going through an unstable season right now: an unstable job, unstable health, unstable relationships. But remember, the Lord who upholds all things upholds you too. The universe hasn't fallen, and neither will you.

Lamentations was written after Jerusalem was destroyed; before the poet's eyes lay nothing but ruins. Yet in the midst of that despair he wrote, “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” What he saw was not the ruins disappearing, but that above the ruins, God's loving kindness still arrived right on time every morning.

Brothers and sisters, your life may look like a pile of ruins right now, but tomorrow morning God's loving kindness will still arrive on time. Just as the sun never refuses to rise because you're in a bad mood, God's faithfulness does not stop because you are weak.

The universe has its ordinances, and our lives also need God's word as their ordinance. The stars have order because they move according to law; our lives have direction when we live according to the Bible. The Bible is my standard: not a reference book, but the dictionary of laws for my life.
The eight steps of changing our mindset
Change in our lives has its “laws” too. We often talk about the eight steps of changing our mindset: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, multiplication.

Notice the later steps: review, correction, repetition. Life change doesn't come from a moment of inspiration; it comes from regular practice. Just as the universe keeps its ordinances every day, we too must practice God's word every day, and our lives will change.

Here's an example: you notice that whenever you get busy, you stop reading the Bible. “Review” is seeing the problem; “correction” is moving your Bible reading to the morning before you leave the house; “repetition” is keeping it up, one day, two days, a whole week. Gradually it stops being a struggle and becomes an ordinance of your life.

God is faithful, and his children must learn faithfulness too. Do what you say, follow through on what you promise, show up on time when you've agreed to meet. Let's become people as reliable as that punctual bus, in our families, our workplaces and our church.

Think about it: in the eyes of your family, coworkers and friends, are you someone reliable? When people say, “Give it to him; I won't have to worry,” that is actually a beautiful testimony. Because through our reliability, people begin to believe that the God we believe in is reliable.
This week's action: set a fixed daily time for devotions, and keep it for seven days in a row. Just as the sun rises on time every day, let your appointment with God be on time every day too.

Tomorrow morning when you see the sunrise, please say one sentence to God: “Great is your faithfulness!”
Let's quietly reflect: God never breaks faith in the universe; how could his promises to me fail?

Your loving kindnesses are new every morning; great is your faithfulness. Just as the sun and moon keep your ordinances, I want to follow you faithfully every day, and let your word be the standard of my life. In Jesus' name, Amen.
