The Story Doesn't End in Heat Death: New Heavens and a New Earth
But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. (2 Peter 3:13)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Have you ever watched a movie where, at the very end, the hero fails, everything is lost, the screen goes black, and the credits start rolling? You sit there in the theater feeling heavy: “That's it? That's how it ends?”

Today we have come to the last stop in the Cosmos Hall. In the earlier units we saw that the universe had a beginning, that the universe is just right, the vastness of the starry sky, the mysteries of light, the furnace of the stars, earth's privileged location, and the ordinances by which the universe keeps its rules. Now we have to ask one last question: how will the story of the universe end?
Science gives us an answer that sounds a bit like that depressing movie. But the Bible gives us a different ending. Today we are going to listen to both, and listen honestly.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. (Matthew 24:35)

In 1998, two teams of astronomers observing distant supernovae made a startling discovery: the universe's expansion is not slowing down but actually speeding up. Three scientists received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for this.
Hot water cools, rooms get messy
The second law of thermodynamics tells us that the usable energy in a closed system keeps decreasing, and disorder, what we call “entropy,” only ever increases.

We all experience this law every day. A hot cup of tea left sitting will always go cold; no cold cup of tea has ever heated itself up. A room left alone will always get messy; no room has ever tidied itself. Parents with kids at home know this law especially well.

Stars are the same: sooner or later their fuel runs out. In about 5 billion years, our sun will swell into a red giant. In the far more distant future, stars in the universe will gradually stop forming, and finally go out one by one.
According to our current understanding, the universe will grow ever colder and darker, until only cold and silence remain. This is called “heat death.”

We should also say honestly that the ultimate fate of the universe depends on the nature of dark energy. Most models predict that the universe will expand forever and gradually cool; some models discuss other possibilities. All of these are projections based on the laws we know, and they are still being studied.
We can picture it like this: the universe is like a wound-up clock that has been ticking since the beginning, its spring slowly unwinding.
This analogy tells us two things. First, it was once wound up, so it has a beginning, and someone who wound it. Second, it will not keep running forever.

They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same. Your years will have no end. (Psalm 102:26–27)
Spiritual meaning: the God who changes the garment

We read this passage back in the first unit, and reading it again now, it takes on a deeper meaning. The psalmist says heaven and earth are wearing out like a garment. But notice: the psalmist doesn't say that when the garment wears out it gets thrown in the trash; he says God will “change them like a cloak.”
The end of an old garment is not nakedness, but putting on new clothes. It is a picture full of hope. The universe will grow old, but God never changes, and his years have no end.
The universe cannot give itself hope
When we talk about heat death, we can't help wondering: then what's the point of everything we do now? If everything ends in cold and silence, are our efforts, our love and our tears all in vain?
That is a very honest question. And we need to answer it honestly: the universe itself cannot offer eternal hope. Hope must come from outside the universe. This is a declaration of faith.
It's like a ship that is slowly sinking: it can't rescue itself using the planks on board. Rescue has to come from outside the ship.

that the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now. (Romans 8:21–22)
Spiritual meaning: hope within the groaning
Paul says the whole creation is groaning and in labor. Hot tea going cold, rooms getting messy, stars going out, bodies growing old: all of this is “the bondage of decay.”

But notice that Paul says creation still hopes to be delivered. The groaning is not a cry of despair; it is like the labor pains before a birth. The pain is real, but behind the pain, new life is coming.

Friends, what in your life is “wearing out”? Perhaps your health, perhaps a relationship, perhaps a dream you once had. The Bible doesn't tell us to pretend it doesn't hurt; it tells us to keep hoping even as we groan.
3. I am making all things new
Now let's look at the ending the Bible writes for the story of the universe.

He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away. He who sits on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” (Revelation 21:4–5)

Friends, this is the difference. Science, based on the laws we know, projects that the universe will end in cold and silence. But the Bible tells us that the Author of the story still has one last word to say: “Behold, I am making all things new.”
The universe had a beginning and is heading toward an end. But the Bible's story does not stop at heat death; it ends in renewal.
The first light of dawn of the new creation
The Lord who gave the universe its beginning will also give it a new beginning. And that new beginning has already begun.

The resurrection of Jesus is the first light of dawn of the new creation. In a universe where everything is wearing out and dying, one body walked out of the tomb, never to die again. It's like the first light appearing in the eastern sky after a long winter night, telling us: dawn is almost here.
Spiritual meaning: in which righteousness dwells
Peter says the new heavens and new earth we look for are a place “in which righteousness dwells.” The new heavens and new earth are not just a more beautiful universe; they are a righteous world.

Today there is so much injustice in the world: people are bullied, people cry out with nowhere to turn. God's righteousness tells us it will not always be this way. The eternal and righteous God will surely make all things new.

Notice that God says, “I am making all things new,” not “I am replacing all things.” God does not throw the old universe away and make a brand-new one from scratch; he is like a master restorer who takes a damaged, faded work that has lost its luster and restores it to be even more glorious than before.

This is a great comfort to us. Our tears today, our love today, what we offer to the Lord today, none of it will be thrown into the universe's trash can. God will wipe away every tear, which means he has seen every single tear. In the new heavens and new earth, nothing done for the Lord will have been in vain.
From a temporary perspective to an eternal one
Since heaven and earth will pass away but God's words will not pass away, we should measure today's gains and losses with the ruler of eternity.

We often worry about things that wear out: cars, houses, reputation, what other people think of us. These are not bad things, but they are all under the second law of thermodynamics; they will all wear out. Only God's word, God's kingdom and human souls last forever.

The Lord Jesus promised, “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne.” We are not meant to grimly hang on in a universe heading for heat death; we are meant to be overcomers in a universe that is about to be made new.
Overcoming does not come from our own strength, but from the fact that the Lord who rose from the dead has already overcome death.

It's like a ball game when you already know the final score. If you knew your team was sure to win in the end, would you panic so much if they were a few points behind at halftime? You'd keep cheering, keep pushing, because you know how it ends. That is what Christian hope is like: we already know the story ends with the new heavens and new earth, so although today's troubles are real, they cannot rob us of our hope.
Welcome the Lord's return: build God's kingdom system

Waiting for the new heavens and new earth doesn't mean sitting around idly. We are to build God's kingdom system and let God's kingdom come in our families and workplaces. The forgiveness we show at home today, our honesty at work, our service in the church: all of it is preparing for the new heavens and new earth, all of it is work done for eternity.
This week's action: write down one thing you will do “for eternity,” and start on it this week.

Brothers and sisters, congratulations on completing the Cosmos Hall! We have traveled all the way from “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” to “Behold, I am making all things new.” We have seen the story of the whole universe, and we have seen the true hero of the story: Jesus Christ.

He is before all things, and in him all things hold together; he entered time, and died and rose again for us; he will come again and make all things new. The movie of the universe does not end with the screen going black; it ends with the beginning of new heavens and a new earth.
Let's quietly reflect: am I living for a heaven and earth that will pass away, or for a kingdom that will last forever?

Eternal Lord, your years have no end. Heaven and earth will all wear out like a garment, but you are the same. I bring before you everything in my life that is wearing out: my body, my relationships, my dreams. Turn my eyes from the temporary to the eternal.
